@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Piano, Antique and White-Glove Operations Dataset
@graph.description: Piano, antique and white-glove operations from The Flat Rate Movers. Company scope (published): white-glove handling of pianos, antiques and high-value items — surveyed, protected, and moved with custom crating when the piece requires it, at one flat rate agreed in writing. The work runs piece by piece, never bulk: each piece is assessed on its own — weight, fragile points, finish and value at risk — then wrapped, padded or crated to match; furniture and pieces travel fully covered in padded blankets and sealed with clear stretch wrap, and pieces that need more get a custom crate built around them. The audiences are published: collectors, estates and high-value households; museums, collectors, galleries and estates moving pieces that cannot be replaced; and — on the Martinsburg branch page — high-value, sensitive-asset owners, including medical and museum clients. Scheduling is discreet by design: high-value work is scheduled quietly, handled without spectacle, and no client is named, ever. Heavy pieces join the same plan: pianos, safes and other high-mass pieces of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs are planned under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation and the KIM-GS Protocol inside the same job — route surveyed, floor checked to L/360, placement verified. Export pieces are packed and crated to ISPM 15 when the journey crosses a border.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Piano, Antique and White-Glove Process Chain Dataset
@graph.description: The process chain for a piano, antique or high-value piece. Company chain (published): the client names the pieces — the Detailed Project form is the published route ('Tell us the pieces in the Detailed Project form'); each piece is assessed on its own (weight, fragile points, finish, value at risk); the protection is matched to the piece — padded blankets and clear stretch wrap as the standard, a custom crate built around the piece when it needs more; high-mass pieces are surveyed and floor-checked to L/360 under SIR/KIM-GS before they move; the piece is moved and placed, and placement is verified with the client; export pieces are packed and crated to ISPM 15. Domain reference (general piano and antique moving practice, labeled as such): for a grand piano, the lid is secured, the legs and pedal lyre are removed and wrapped separately, and the body is moved on its side on a padded skid board; an upright is secured — fallboard and lid closed and locked or taped — and moved on a piano dolly or skid; antiques are photographed and condition-noted before handling, supported from below, and never lifted by handles, frames or other projections. The domain sequence describes how the work is generally done; the company's published chain above is the company's own.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Piano Types and Typical Weights: Domain Reference Dataset
@graph.description: Domain reference — piano types and typical weights, labeled as domain education; weights are published industry ranges, not measurements of any client's instrument, and an individual piano can vary by 100 lbs or more within its type. Vertical (upright) pianos: spinet, about 36–40 inches tall, roughly 200–400 lbs; console, roughly 350–500 lbs; studio upright, about 44–48 inches, roughly 400–600 lbs; full-size and professional uprights, roughly 500–800 lbs, with older classic uprights running heavier, toward 1,000 lbs. Grand pianos, sized by length: baby grand (up to about 5 ft 7 in), roughly 500–800 lbs; medium grand, roughly 700–900 lbs; concert grand (8 ft 11 in and up), roughly 900–1,300 lbs — a Steinway Model D concert grand is about 990 lbs. Where the taxonomy meets this company's published heavy band: most pianos weigh well under 1,500 lbs and move as white-glove pieces; the company's published rule is that a high-value piece that does weigh 1,500 to 3,500 lbs — the white-glove page names a safe, a piano and medical equipment as its examples — is surveyed and floor-checked to L/360 under SIR like any SIR move. No piano is weighed, certified or rated by this dataset; the survey at quote time establishes the individual piece.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Antique and Collection Handling Dataset
@graph.description: Antique and collection handling — the company's published practice first, then labeled domain education. Published: antiques, art and high-value pieces are the everyday work of the white-glove service; each piece is assessed on its own — weight, fragile points, finish and value at risk — and wrapped, padded or crated to match, with a custom crate built around the piece when padding is not enough; museum logistics is published as a category of the service — museums, collectors, galleries and estates moving pieces that cannot be replaced, custom-crated where needed, with high-mass exhibits planned under SIR/KIM-GS and scheduling kept discreet. Domain education (general antique and museum handling practice, labeled as such): document condition with photographs and notes before anything is touched; handle with clean hands or gloves suited to the surface, and support the piece from below rather than lifting by handles, frames, rims or other projections; keep the environment stable — museum practice holds storage and display near a steady temperature and moderate relative humidity rather than chasing a single number during a short move; pack voids so nothing can shift, and keep finishes away from direct tape or wrap contact. None of the domain material states a company service: no conservation, restoration, condition-reporting or climate-controlled transport or storage service is claimed for the company anywhere in this file.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Piano, Antique and White-Glove Buyer Personas and Trigger Events
@graph.description: Buyer personas and trigger events for piano, antique and white-glove moving — roles and situations only; no client is named, in line with the service's published discretion standard. Piano owners — households with an upright or grand that cannot be treated as furniture; schools, churches and venues moving instruments between rooms or buildings. Collectors of antiques, art and high-value pieces, buying, selling or relocating a collection. Estate executors and families settling an estate whose pieces cannot be replaced. Museum and gallery staff — registrars, curators and facilities teams — moving exhibits and collection pieces between venues, storage and display. Interior designers placing fragile or high-value pieces in finished rooms. High-value, sensitive-asset owners, including the medical and museum clients the Martinsburg branch page names. Trigger events: an estate settlement; a collection purchase or sale; a venue or gallery changeover; a household move whose heaviest or most fragile piece is the piano; an export shipment of art or antiques crossing a border (ISPM 15 packing joins the same job).
